# Segmentation and Visualization: Additional Examples

{{< include "includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

---

This short chapter collects a few additional examples that round out the
visualization pipeline introduced over the previous two chapters: iso-voxel
resampling, gray/white segmentation tools, and the practical benefit of
averaging multiple scans before segmenting. The overall pipeline these three
chapters trace runs from raw voxels, through gray/white segmentation, to
surface boundaries (marching cubes), surface smoothing, and finally flat
maps.

## Gray-white segmentation is essential

Every step in the surface-construction pipeline — meshing, smoothing,
flattening — depends on an accurate gray/white matter segmentation as its
starting point. Overlaying a sampling grid on an unsegmented axial slice (a)
versus the same slice with the gray/white boundary traced (b) makes clear how
much structure the segmentation step adds before any surface computation can
begin (@fig-ch69-graywhite-segmentation-essential).

![(a) An axial slice with a sampling grid overlaid, before segmentation. (b)
The same slice with the gray/white matter boundary
traced.](images/ch69/graywhite-segmentation-essential.png){#fig-ch69-graywhite-segmentation-essential}

Segmentation is typically done with dedicated tools such as itkGray (built on
ITK-SNAP), which let a user inspect a volume in multiple planes
simultaneously, draw and edit labels, and preview the resulting 3D region
(@fig-ch69-itkgray-segmentation-tool).

![itkGray (built on ITK-SNAP), a segmentation tool showing axial, sagittal,
and coronal views alongside a 3D
preview.](images/ch69/itkgray-segmentation-tool.png){#fig-ch69-itkgray-segmentation-tool}

## Voxel size and resampling

Scanner voxels are frequently anisotropic — for example, $0.9375 \times
0.9375 \times 1.2$ mm — and if the image is displayed without accounting for
this, each measurement sample simply becomes one image pixel and the brain
appears artificially "thin" (@fig-ch69-original-scan-anisotropic-voxels).

![The original scan represented as voxels with no scaling applied: each
sample is one pixel, so the anisotropic $0.9375 \times 0.9375 \times 1.2$~mm
voxels make the brain look
thin.](images/ch69/original-scan-anisotropic-voxels.png){#fig-ch69-original-scan-anisotropic-voxels}

Resampling to an isotropic (iso-)voxel size — for example, $0.9 \times 0.9
\times 0.9$ mm — corrects this distortion, at the cost of introducing
interpolation noise (@fig-ch69-resampled-iso-voxel). Standard scattered-data
and grid interpolation routines (such as MATLAB's `interp2` for 2D reslicing
and `TriScatteredInterp` for scattered 3D data) are the practical tools used
to perform this resampling.

![Resampled to an isotropic $0.9 \times 0.9 \times 0.9$~mm voxel grid — note
the interpolation noise introduced in the
process.](images/ch69/resampled-iso-voxel.png){#fig-ch69-resampled-iso-voxel}

## Averaging multiple scans improves segmentation

Co-registering and averaging several repeated scans of the same subject
reduces noise substantially before any segmentation is attempted
(@fig-ch69-coregistered-averaged-scans).

![Multiple scans of the same subject, co-registered and
averaged.](images/ch69/coregistered-averaged-scans.png){#fig-ch69-coregistered-averaged-scans}

The benefit shows up directly in the intensity histogram used to separate
gray and white matter: averaging sharpens the separation between the gray and
white matter intensity peaks, making automatic segmentation more reliable
(@fig-ch69-averaging-improves-segmentation-histograms).

![Averaging multiple scans sharpens the separation between gray- and
white-matter intensity peaks, making segmentation
easier.](images/ch69/averaging-improves-segmentation-histograms.png){#fig-ch69-averaging-improves-segmentation-histograms}
